In-Sensor Touch Analysis for Intent Recognition

Yijing Xu, 
Shifan Yu,

Abstract

Tactile intent recognition systems, which are highly desired to satisfy human's needs and humanized services, shall be accurately understanding and identifying human's intent. They generally utilize time-driven sensor arrays to achieve high spatiotemporal resolution, however, which encounter inevitable challenges of low scalability, huge data volumes, and complex processing. Here, an event-driven intent recognition touch sensor (IR touch sensor) with in-sensor computing capability is presented. The merit of event-driven and in-sensor computing enables the IR touch sensor to achieve ultrahigh resolution and obtain complete intent information with intrinsic concise data. It achieves critical signal extraction of action trajectories with a rapid response time of 0.4 ms and excellent durability of >10 000 cycles, bringing an important breakthrough of tactile intent recognition. Versatile applications prove the integrated functions of the IR touch sensor for great interactive potential in all-weather environments regardless of shading, dynamics, darkness, and noise. Unconscious and even hidden action features can be perfectly extracted with the ultrahigh recognition accuracy of 98.4% for intent recognition. The further auxiliary diagnostic test demonstrates the practicability of the IR touch sensor in telemedicine palpation and therapy. This groundbreaking integration of sensing, data reduction, and ultrahigh-accuracy recognition will propel the leapfrog development for conscious machine intelligence.

1 Introduction

Intent recognition is the process of inferring the human's intent or purposes by analyzing their language, actions, or other perceptual inputs so that the interactive objects, such as robots, can satisfy human's needs or provide humanized services. It possesses broad development prospects in healthcare,[1-6] human–machine interaction,[7-14] intelligent robots,[15-18] etc. Nevertheless, recognizing human's intent information poses significant challenges due to its inherent complexity and abstraction. In addressing this challenge, machine intelligence has become a crucial means to achieve intent recognition.[19] Relying on signals collected through sensors, machines can access more comprehensive and urate information so as to strengthen their understanding and recognition capabilities of human's intent. Researchers are dedicated to investigating sensors across different perceptual dimensions to advance machine intelligence,[20-23] enabling better understanding and interpretation of human's intent in increasingly complex and diverse scenarios. Nonetheless, intent recognition systems based on visual sensors, such as pattern recognition and text recognition, will be susceptible to interference from external light conditions and pose challenges to their performance in varying lighting environments.[24-26] Auditory intent recognition systems, like speech recognition, may experience a decrease in recognition accuracy due to external environmental sounds, introducing challenges in accurate recognition in noisy surroundings.[27, 28] Compared to other sensing systems, tactile intent recognition systems are free from the surrounding environment, as tactile perception relies on direct physical contact with objects or surfaces. It will make systems less susceptible to changes in lighting, sound, or other external factor.[24] Furthermore, tactile perception is required for most operational systems to provide contact parameters,[29-31] such as velocity and direction of sliding, contact location, duration, and frequency, allowing objective entities to draw inserted high-level information and execute corresponding actions in the interaction process.[32]

Ideally, touch sensors for intent recognition should be easily scalable and allow for on-demand spatial distribution. Furthermore, they should minimize wiring requirements without compromising the transmission of touch information.[33] However, touch sensors covering the robot body for tactile perception and recognition of human intent may be discrete. Due to a trade-off between high spatial resolution and device manufacturing complexity, data acquisition, and data processing, intent recognition touch sensors based on the array of sensing units are unable to cover large areas with high spatiotemporal resolution while simultaneously outputting low-dimensional signals.[34] First, increasing the density of the sensor array and the quantity of sensing units normally requires a larger number of connection wires,[35] posing challenges for device manufacturing.[36-40] Meanwhile, intent recognition touch sensors with high spatial resolution output signals in high dimensions, which generally carry large amounts of meaningless information regardless of the presence or absence of external stimulation.[29, 41-43] Moreover, discrete sensing units can only output temporal series without fusing spatial information. Thus, it is imperative to transmit temporal series to the computing terminal for spatial information fusion. Due to the separation of sensing units and computing terminals, the movement of substantial data between them leads to latency.[44-48] While the limited volume of data generated by a small number of sensing units can expedite backend processing and analysis, this may lead to the omission of crucial information that prevents the accurate identification of true intent. With the increase in array resolution, it has the privilege to distill comprehensive cognition of interaction intent from output high-dimension signals.[35, 49] However, fusing a large amount of data and extracting valuable information necessitates complex algorithms that undoubtedly add to the burden of backend analysis and processing.[41] Balancing the need for concise data with the inclusion of accurate intent information appears to be a seemingly irreconcilable paradox.

Here, we propose an event-driven intent recognition touch sensor, termed IR touch sensor, striving to realize complex intent recognition through in-sensor touch analysis. The IR touch sensor is composed of the biomimetic helical web, which innovatively combines low dimensions of signals and ultrahigh precision spatiotemporal resolution into the same device by connecting separated pixel points. This design allows the device to scale the resolution extension based on application requirements while maintaining a constant number of electrodes. The IR touch sensor utilizes “external stimulation” as the event that drives the start of data acquisition and transmission, effectively eliminating redundant data in the sensing process. Through analysis and computing within the sensor, it efficiently integrates spatial information into temporal signals in the form of amplitude features. The IR touch sensor can establish a linear relationship between the output signal and the stimulation location, directly outputting a 1D fusion signal. This in-sensor computing ability minimizes the transfer of redundant data between the sensing units and computing terminal, so which reduces the complexity of data processing and conversion. These merits enhance the serviceability and dependability of the IR touch sensor in capturing and analyzing touch intent cues. Relying on this linear relationship, decoding the output signal of the IR touch sensor enables the successful extraction of action trajectories for the accurate recognition of human's intent. Compared to the commercial resistive touch screen, the IR touch sensor exhibits superior performance, making it more suitable for various application scenarios. Typical applications of PowerPoint presentations, navigation of an electronic map, and manipulation of game objects are achieved to demonstrate the bending insensitivity and decouplable sliding operation characteristics of the IR touch sensor, which possesses great interactive potential in all-weather environments regardless of shading, dynamics, darkness, and noise. Furthermore, a machine-learning-assisted intelligent handwriting recognition system is presented to show the practicability of the IR touch sensor in telemedicine palpation and treatment. This work provides new insights into tactile intent recognition with conscious machine intelligence, which may find wide applications in wearable devices, smart robots, medical palpation and therapy, and so on.

2 Result

2.1 Design Concept of the IR Touch Sensor

Intent recognition is an advanced technique for analyzing human's intent, motivations, and expectations, enabling computer systems to understand and respond more intelligently to their behaviors. In the field of human–robot interaction, tactile intent recognition plays a key role in providing users with a more natural and intuitive experience. For instance, people could communicate with the robot by touching the array of discrete sensing units on the external surface of the robot's body (Figure 1a). Robots can directly recognize human's thoughts through touch. The number of tactile sensing units and their distribution across the robot surface can influence the quality of measurement and eventually impact the effectiveness of recognition results.[3] Generally, the biomimetic robot's fingers are equipped with the highest resolution sensor array, while the resolution of the sensor array on the robot's back is comparatively lower. The resolution of the sensor array on the robot's arms lies between them. The distribution of these touch-sensing units mimics the hierarchy of mechanosensory distribution of the human body.[33, 50] Figure 1b shows the common flow chart that the robot perceives a sliding path via a sensor array to extract the human's intent. Numerous sensing signals from the sensor array will be processed into fusion signals by the microcontroller unit. Subsequently, the fusion signal is transmitted to a computing terminal to analyze touch information and then processed by a neural network to identify human's intent. Tactile intent recognition could be applied in presentation, navigation, entertainment, handwriting recognition, and more, showing great potential in the aspects of artificial intelligence of things (Figure 1c). Specifically, when humans transmit their intent by sliding along a specific path on a robot's palm, for example, “Z” (Figure 1d), the sustained time signals are altered by external stimulation. However, the low scalability and complex wiring of sensor arrays stem the advance of high-resolution tactile intent recognition systems.

In the biological world, spiders use the least amount of mucus to weave their webs with the most area coverage (Figure 1e-i). The spider web is a product of evolutionary adaptation that can effectively convey information about the nature and location of the vibration sources produced by prey collisions. The spider web mainly consists of radial threads that build the frame and spirals threads that connect adjacent radial threads.[51] The rapid transmission of vibration signals to spiders for prey orientation can be achieved due to the junctions between the adjacent radial threads by spirals threads. This arrangement facilitates the rapid transmission of information to neighboring regions, enabling the efficient interplanar transfer of signals. Inspired by the spiral structure of the spider web, we proposed and designed the biomimetic helical web that winds all separated sensing units in a spiral configuration (Figure 1e-ii). It would establish the widest perception domain with the simplest wiring, which significantly enhanced the flexibility and scalability of tactile intent recognition devices. Based on this design, we fabricated the event-driven IR touch sensor, which exhibited a linear relationship between the output signal and the stimulation location and allowed for in-sensor computing and output decoding of the touch location.

Commonly, when using the array of discrete sensing units to implement tactile intent recognition in a specific area, it is still a challenge to balance concise data with high resolution and high accuracy (Figure 1f). For instance, a sensor array with low sensing unit density, such as 2 × 2 resolution, is easy to manufacture and simplifies the back-end processing and analysis due to fewer dimensions of output signals. The confined signals and the insufficient resolution may make it difficult to fully encompass tactile information, thus posing challenges in accurately recognizing tactile intents. An alternative way is to increase sensing unit density (such as 7 × 7 resolution), which can improve touch resolution to enhance the accuracy of interactive intent recognition. However, this way seems to inevitably increase the dimensionality of signals, bring more redundant data, significantly increase processing difficulty, and reduce the efficiency of analysis and processing. In addition, the operating mechanism of these sensor arrays is almost time-driven, which conveys time-domain signals with a fixed time interval regardless of whether the status of the sensor array changing or not. This time-driven operating mechanism results in the generation of a substantial amount of redundant data with limited information and increasing the movement of redundant data between sensing units and computing terminals. To effectively process these data, complex algorithms are required to integrate spatial information and temporal signals, presenting the backend processing and analysis with increasingly complex challenges and difficulties. In this work, the proposed IR touch sensor overcame these challenges by the design of a biomimetic helical web, coupled with its in-sensor computing capability and event-driven operating mechanism. The biomimetic helical web established pixel connections across the sensing surface, enhancing local correlation and significantly reducing the dimensions of output signals at the device level while maintaining a considerable level of resolution. The event-driven operating mechanism enabled the IR touch sensor to generate output signals only when external stimulation was applied. It effectively reduced the generation of redundant data and made the data concise and effective during the sensing process. What's more, the IR touch sensor performed touch analysis directly within the sensor, fused temporal signals and spatial information, and then output a 1D fusion signal. This ability of in-sensor computing minimized the transfer of redundant data between the sensor and external circuitry while still sustaining high-accuracy tactile intent recognition. Therefore, the proposed IR touch sensor offered significant advantages in recognition accuracy, outputting 1D and concise signal, and computational efficiency.

2.2 Performance and Characteristics of Tapping and Sliding Touch

The structure of the IR touch sensor was hierarchically illustrated in Figure 2a-i, which consisted of five stacking thin layers of two polyethylene terephthalate (PET) films as the upper and bottom substrates, two biomimetic helical web conductive patterns, and the spacer. Conductive ink was applied to the PET substrate to prepare the conductive patterns as the biomimetic helical web through screen printing. Then, these two parts were face-to-face put together with a thin spacer. Due to the pixel interconnections across the sensing surface, the upper and bottom conductive patterns served as both the sensing unit and the conduction pathway. In the profile diagram, it could be observed that the upper and bottom conductive patterns were separated when no external stimulation was applied on the IR touch sensor (Figure 2a-ii). Therefore, in the noncontact state, the upper and lower conductive patterns were not in breakover. Once an external stimulation, such as a finger touch, was applied on the IR touch sensor, the upper and bottom conductive patterns contacted together at the stimulation location. In this triggered state, a connection between the upper and bottom conductive patterns was established. The electrons started from the upper conductive pattern and the stimulation location to the bottom conductive pattern to form a complete transmission path. Depending on the stimulation location, the length of the conductive pathway varied, leading to differences in the value of the output signal. Figure S1 (Supporting Information) detailed the sensing mechanism of the IR touch sensor. This operating mechanism ensured the differentiated response of the IR touch sensor, allowing customization of the output signal for different control requirements. This also confirmed that the IR touch sensor was event-driven. When the IR touch sensor was integrated into the circuit, an electrical signal was generated once the touch exceeded a predetermined threshold, marking the start of data acquisition and transmission. The advantage of this mechanism was that the system processed data only when touch events occurred. It would reduce the computing resource wastage, and could immediately respond to touch events, providing real-time feedback. However, achieving multi-point touch sensing on the IR touch sensor with two electrodes required a more elaborate mechanism to handle this challenge. In addition, the biomimetic helical web conductive patterns were scalable and allowed to be designed and customized for the construction of the IR touch sensor to achieve large-area coverage with high spatiotemporal resolution, for the particular requirements of individual users or specific tasks; this included adjusting the line width, line interval, and pattern width of the biomimetic helical web (Figure S2a, Supporting Information). To validate the feasibility and stability of the biomimetic helical web conductive patterns, four styles of IR touch sensors were devised featuring different sizes of the biomimetic helical web conductive patterns, referred to as Style I, Style II, Style III, and Style IV. Detailed information about these IR touch sensors was available in Table S1. The conceptual diagrams and photographs could be referenced in Figure S2b (Supporting Information).

To facilitate signal acquisition, the IR touch sensor was connected in parallel with a load resistor, forming the measurement circuit (Figure S3a, Supporting Information). By detecting the electrical signals of the measurement circuit, such as resistance and current, the resistance variation of the IR touch sensor could be calculated, thereby reflecting the touch location on the IR touch sensor. Therefore, a series of resistors were chosen to be connected in parallel with different styles of IR touch sensors to find out the most suitable load resistor. The relative changes in resistance (ΔR/R0) of the measurement circuit were tested at different touch locations for a series of IR touch sensors with different load resistors (Figure 2b-i; Figure S4, Supporting Information). The change curves demonstrated a consistent variation trend for different load resistors. The minimum relative change in resistance and range of relative change in resistance of the measurement circuit extracted from the curve indicated that the optimal load resistor differed for four style IR touch sensors (Style I ≈ 56 kΩ, Style II ≈ 100 kΩ, Style III ≈ 56 kΩ, and Style IV ≈ 100 kΩ). This was due to the different inherent resistance of these IR touch sensors. Overall, the wider the range of the relative change and the larger the minimum relative change, the signal would be more pronounced in subsequent performance testing and practical applications (Figure 2b-ii). Thus, the subsequent performance measurements were based on the Style I IR touch sensor in parallel with a 100 kΩ resistor unless otherwise stated.

To optimize the mechanical properties of the IR touch sensor, a series of IR touch sensors with different thickness spacers were fabricated and their response pressure threshold analysis was conducted (Figure 2c). The total resistance of the circuit was 100 kΩ when no external force was applied. As the external force increased, the upper and bottom conductive patterns progressively approached and eventually contacted saturation. At this point, the overall resistance of the circuit immediately decreased to a stable value, which did not vary with the increase of the external force. The results showed that the thinner the spacer was, the external force was less required to achieve saturation. The influence of thickness on the response time of the IR touch sensor was further investigated by loading and unloading (Figure 2d). The response time was for the IR touch sensor to obtain a stable output signal and the recovery time was that of the signal returned to initial state. As shown in Figure S3b (Supporting Information), the corresponding voltage response across the load resistor was measured. The response times of the IR touch sensors with three spacer thicknesses, including 0.27, 0.4, and 0.55 mm, were determined to be 0.4, 0.8, and 1.5 ms, respectively. Evidently, the increase in spacer thickness resulted in an extended time to transition from the separated state (initial noncontact state) to the saturation state (fully contact state) during the force loading process. Correspondingly, the recovery times were 0.5, 1.4, and 1.6 ms, respectively. The relevant response curves for the IR touch sensors with different spacer thicknesses were depicted in Figure 2e and Figure S5a (Supporting Information). From the curves, the response signal of the IR touch sensor rapidly reached saturation with the external force. Due to the elastic deformation of the spacer, there was a slight hysteresis during unloading, resulting in a slightly higher recovery time compared to response time. When the spacer thickness was 0.27 mm, the IR touch sensor kept low hysteresis, which was beneficial to the consistency and reliability in dynamic measurements.[38] Therefore, the spacer of 0.27 mm thickness was selected for the subsequent fabrication of the IR touch sensors with different types. The corresponding response and recovery times were measured (Figure S5b, Supporting Information). Furthermore, the surface morphology of the junction between the spacer and the conductive pattern was characterized by laser confocal scanning microscopy and scanning electron microscope (Figure S6, Supporting Information), which verified the 0.27 mm thickness of the spacer (Figures S7a,b, Supporting Information). The section structure of the IR touch sensor could be clearly observed in Figure S7c (Supporting Information). It validated that in the absence of external force, the upper and bottom conductive patterns were isolated by the spacer.

To extract hidden information from the output signal, the relationship between the output signal and the stimulation location should be quantified. The IR touch sensor exhibited a good linearity between them with an R2 value of 0.99929 (Figure S8, Supporting Information). As a result, the IR touch sensor could output the corresponding electrical signals under external mechanical stimulation, realizing the unique transformation from location information to electrical signals. It laid the important foundation for accurate tactile intent recognition. Figure 2f-i revealed the schematic of the touch locations (from L1 to L6) of the IR touch sensor for testing the spatiotemporal dynamic response. The result indicated a high level of differentiation in dynamic response to temporal and spatial mechanical stimulation (Figure 2f-ii). Considering the diverse habits from different users, the impact of rapid and long-term touch operations on the output signal was investigated (Figure 2g). The mechanical stimulation of varying durations of 1, 5, and 8 s was employed. The result manifested when the loading duration was increased, the corresponding response signals of the IR touch sensor were always stable. Its relative rate of change in response signal did not exceed 1%. Furthermore, multiple cyclic tests on the IR touch sensor were conducted with different durations (Figure S9, Supporting Information). The response signal demonstrated excellent repeatable features. The bending of the IR touch sensor during usage posed a potential challenge as it could interfere with the IR touch sensor's sensing characteristics.[52] To address this concern, the response signal of the IR touch sensor at three locations was tested at different radii (Figure 2h). It was found that when the IR touch sensor was attached to a curved surface, the change in the response signal was very slight. As the bending radius changed from 20 to 100 mm, the resistance of the IR touch sensor remained essentially stable, with L1 measuring ≈2.5 kΩ, L2 ≈ 20 kΩ, and L3 ≈ 14 kΩ (Figure 2h-i). The range of resistance variation did not exceed 0.1% (Figure 2h-ii). Encouragingly, the degrees of attenuation were minimal and could be disregarded, which verified the strong anti-interference ability of the IR touch sensor. The durability of the IR touch sensor was detected by a repetitive loading–unloading test for more than 10 000 cycles (Figure 2i). The response signal was almost unchanged, exhibiting excellent stability and robustness of the IR touch sensor. Compared to the commercial five-wire resistive touch screen, the IR touch sensor demonstrated superior performance in terms of response time, sensitivity, bending insensitivity, and cost control, which better met the needs of different application scenarios (Table S2, Note S1, Supporting Information).

More importantly, the IR touch sensor could decouple continuous sliding operations, which was not directly available in the commercial five-wire resistive touch screen. Furthermore, the output characteristics with different sliding operations were investigated. Figures 3a and S10 (Supporting Information) illustrated the results of the continuous and discontinuous sliding operations, respectively. Continuous sliding referred to sliding along the conductive pattern, where the output signal changed continuously (Figure S10, Supporting Information). Discontinuous sliding referred to sliding across the conductive pattern. The signal from discontinuous sliding was intermittent, it offered more flexible control in specific operations, such as when quick command switching was required (Figure 3a). The IR touch sensor, benefiting from its helical structure, effectively combined these two types of sliding, thereby broadening the range of applications. Subsequently, a comparative analysis of the sliding output response was conducted to assess the impact of different winding shapes, including helical shape and S shape (Figure 3b). When the finger slid along the same path on the IR touch sensor using these two winding shapes, the output response of the IR touch sensor based on the helical shape exhibited greater spatial distinctiveness. Taking D1, D2, and D3 path differences formed between adjacent two points during the sliding process as an example, it was evident that in the helical shape, the values of D1, D2, and D3 were not equal, with the path difference first decreasing and then increasing. In contrast, the path differences for the S-shaped winding remained nearly unchanged. This conductive path difference directly affected the variation in electrical signals. Figure 3c and Figure S11 (Supporting Information) depicted the output signals of the two winding shapes sliding along the diagonal, while also extracting the difference between adjacent peaks as an evaluation metric. The difference in the output signals based on the helical shape went down first and then went up in the opposite direction. The uneven path differences resulted in greater variation between adjacent peaks of the output signal, which provided more distinct features, making the detection of touch locations more precise. For the S-shaped winding, the variation between adjacent peaks of the output signal was relatively small due to the path difference remaining almost constant at certain locations. This was disadvantageous for signal processing and analysis, as smaller variations reduced the accuracy of touch location detection. This further verified the advantage in the structural design of the biomimetic helical web, enhancing the spatial resolution and uniqueness of the output signals. Therefore, the IR touch sensor using the helical shape could enhance the accuracy of tactile intent recognition.

Based on the previous results, the IR touch sensor showed high linearity in touch perception (Figure S8, Supporting Information). It indicated that there was a clear mathematical and physical relationship between the output signal and the stimulation location. Thereby, this relationship could be represented in the form of the resistance heatmap that displayed the resistance values at each location (Figure S12a, Supporting Information), which would serve to decode the output signals and then obtain the sliding path. Figure 3d provided the change in response resistance of the measurement circuit when sliding along the IR touch sensor with different paths, including lateral slide and oblique slide. As the measurement circuit was realized by the IR touch sensor in parallel with the load resistor (Figure S3a, Supporting Information), the IR touch sensor's resistance (Rsensor) could be decoded as:

By calculating each peak in the output signal, a sequence of decoded resistance values could be obtained. Subsequently, projecting these values onto the resistance heatmap allowed for the decoding of the sliding path. In Figure S12b (Supporting Information), resistance responses and decoded output for two other paths were also presented. The decoding capability across the entire area ensured that the IR touch sensor could accurately capture and convey the accurate motion trajectory, contributing to its effectiveness in diverse interactive intent recognition applications. Figure 3f and Figure S12c (Supporting Information) displayed the output signals when the finger slid along the IR touch sensor from left to right with different velocities. The sliding velocities could be measured by Equation 2, where S was fixed at 70 mm and Δt was obtained from the output signals. The specific durations were Δt1 = 2.576 s, Δt2 = 11.811 s, Δt3 = 6.018 s, and Δt4 = 1.733 s. Consequently, the calculated sliding velocities were ≈v1 = 27.174 mm s−1, v2 = 5.927 mm s−1, v3 = 11.632 mm s−1, and v4 = 40.392 mm s−1, respectively. It could be found that although sliding at different velocities, the relative change in current was almost not affected by velocity, that is, in the range of <1% (Figure 3g), which indicated the reliability of the IR touch sensor across various sliding velocities, making it suitable for a wide range of interactive scenarios and accommodating users with diverse usage habits. The output signals of four styles of IR touch sensors, sliding laterally back and forth along the same path, are shown in Figure S13 (Supporting Information). Here, the impact of parameter designs of the biomimetic helical web conductive pattern on output signals was assessed in three dimensions: peak duration time, the interval time between peaks, and the number of peaks. The density of the output signal by different types of IR touch sensors was closely related to the device resolution (Figure S14, Supporting Information). Moreover, reliability and stability were also important criteria for evaluating the performance of the IR touch sensor. The durability test was conducted to demonstrate the long sliding life of the IR touch sensor (Figure 3h; Figure S15, Supporting Information). In both cases of continuous sliding and discontinuous sliding, the output signal of the IR touch sensor was stable and repeatable even over 10 000 cycles. Therefore, the IR touch sensor had great potential applications in tactile intent recognition because of its fast response time, bending insensitivity, and high-cyclic stability, which ensured accurate sensing of tactile intent via converted output signals in real time.

2.3 Broad Applicability of the Biomimetic Helical Web

In the domain of tactile intent recognition, the appropriateness of the common sensor array with different resolutions varies depending on the scenarios. For instance, consider the recognition of handwriting letters “L” and “O”. When the letters were written on the common sensor array, the output signals were analyzed and processed to obtain the decoded output. Subsequently, the intended input could be identified based on this decoding output. The letter “L” could be accurately detected using a common sensor array with the 3 × 3 resolution (Figure 4a-i), but the letter “O” encountered difficulties at this lower resolution. This might result in wrong classifications, such as being recognized as the letter “D” (Figure 4a-ii). Nevertheless, increasing the resolution to 11 × 11 enabled accurate recognition of the input letter “O” (Figure 4a-ii). Given the diverse nature of intent recognition scenarios, the applicability of the biomimetic helical web was regarded as a means to address various perception requirements (Figure 4b). The biomimetic helical web commenced from the sensing unit positioned in the first row and column of the common sensor array, winding clockwise from the outermost to the innermost layers to ensure passing each sensing unit. This design not only guaranteed consistent resolution but also significantly reduced manufacturing complexity and enhanced scalability. Therefore, regardless of their specifications, common sensor arrays, irrespective of the resolution, could be dimensionality reduced into biomimetic helical webs at the device level, encompassing configurations of odd × odd, even × even, odd × even, and even × odd. Several typical common sensor arrays and their corresponding dimension-reduced biomimetic helical webs were enumerated, including odd × odd (3 × 3), even × even (6 × 6), odd × even (4 × 7), and even × odd (9 × 6). The successful transformation of these diverse configurations highlighted the applicability of the biomimetic helical web to varied sensor array specifications, regardless of the arrangement of the sensing units.

A challenge was that simply increasing the resolution of sensor arrays would result in heightened dimensions of output signals. During the intent recognition, the output sensing signals often necessitated additional extraction and processing to generate fusion signals for subsequent decoding (Figure 4c-i). While the increase in dimensions of the output signal contributed to a rise in redundant data, accompanied by heightened computational costs for external processing.[53] Therefore, to ensure the efficient transmission of tactile intent, touch sensors must be adaptively scaled across resolution requirements. The biomimetic helical web maintained the output of the IR touch sensor as a 1D fusion signal. This signal was calculated within the sensors and directly outputted, which could be utilized for obtaining decoded output. (Figure 4c-ii). Common sensor arrays often involved complex post-processing to fuse signals from multiple sensing units, bringing potential latency. However, the biomimetic helical web could address this challenge by incorporating computational capabilities within individual sensors. This distinction underscored the efficiency of biomimetic helical webs in minimizing signal redundancy while upholding accuracy in intent recognition. The conciseness of the output signal, coupled with its inclusion of all tactile information, enhanced computational efficiency and facilitated robust real-time processing. This further emphasized the advantages of biomimetic helical webs in the fabrication of IR touch sensors for tactile intent recognition. Accurate intent recognition could be achieved across the biomimetic helical web with various resolutions, by integrating the location information into the output signals. Figure 4d and Figure S16 (Supporting Information) illustrated the decoding process of time-domain signals for the IR touch sensors made of the biomimetic helical webs at different resolutions. Real-time time-domain signals were continuously output only when the IR touch sensor suffered the sliding touch. By analyzing the feature map and locating the highest point of the curve, the decoding output could be extracted, which was highly consistent with the slide path (Figure 4d-i). It was worth noting that whether whatever resolution was required, biomimetic helical webs could be employed to construct IR touch sensors. These IR touch sensors excelled in tactile intent recognition (Figure 4d-ii). This strategic incorporation of location information and output signal heightened the reliability of intent recognition, enabling accurate recognition across diverse resolutions. Thus, the biomimetic helical web presented a dual applicability which was exemplified in its structural applicability to various sensor array configurations and for accurate tactile intent recognition at different resolution requirements. These findings were promising for effectively conveying spatial and temporal information and for using IR touch sensors to transfer the intent of physical touch interactions.

2.4 Typical Applications of Touch Interactions

Due to the sensing capability of different operations, such as single-point touch and sliding, the IR touch sensor could serve as a versatile interface for tactile intent recognition toward potential applications in gaming, education, healthcare, and smart furniture. Leveraging accurate decoding of output signals and the broad applicability of biomimetic helical web, a range of applications based on the IR touch sensors with different resolutions were developed, demonstrating the bending insensitivity of the IR touch sensor as well as its fast response ability and versatility. Figure 5a illustrated the schematics of the overall process from transmission to recognition for tactile intent. Specifically, when users aimed to initiate control operations, either slide or tap actions were performed on the IR touch sensor, which would generate real-time fusion signals. Here, an external circuit was established to streamline signal collection, conversion, and transmission (Figure S17, Supporting Information). Guided by a pre-set program, the backend interactive system could effectively identify the corresponding operational commands, resulting in successful intent recognition as well as subsequent action performance.

The IR touch sensor with 3 × 3 resolution was designed specifically for controlling PowerPoint presentations (Figure 5b). Four distinct locations of the IR touch sensor corresponded to the actions of the slide show, end, previous slide, and next slide, respectively (Figure 5b-i). Based on the bending-insensitive property of the IR touch sensor (Figure 2h), it could reliably adhere to the irregular surfaces of the human body without causing any signal interference. Thus, the user's control intent could be accurately recognized for efficient operation in presentation scenarios. The output signals of the “next slide” command and the others were shown in Figure 5b-ii and Figure S18a (Supporting Information), respectively. The output signals of these four operations accurately corresponded to distinct locations in the resolution array, ensuring the accurate control of PowerPoint presentations. This layout guaranteed the dependability of every command, hence enhancing the entire efficiency of tactile intent recognition. The snapshots and demo of controlling the PowerPoint presentations through the IR touch sensor were presented in Figure 5b-iii and Movie S1 (Supporting Information), respectively. The bending-insensitive characteristic of the IR touch sensor made it suitable for many screen-unsuitable applications, such as wearable control panels embedded in flexible fabrics, skin patches, etc. Compared with the traditional rigid screen, the IR touch sensor could provide users with a more comfortable experience.

Next, the ability of the IR touch sensor to decouple sliding signals and extract motion paths through the application program was demonstrated. By sliding along a specified path on the IR touch sensor with 11 × 11 resolution, the navigation of an electronic map was successfully achieved to implement the real-time and continuous operations of “sliding – sensing – computing – judging – action”, which eliminated the need for mice and keyboards (Figure 5c). Initially, a baseline was established and then six different angles and lengths were selected for sliding, which were intended to roll up, roll down, roll right, and roll left, as well as zoom in and out, on the electronic map. A detailed reference could be found in Figure S18b (Supporting Information). By analyzing the output signals, whether their minimum values fell within the predetermined range were evaluated. If it fell, the backend interactive system allowed to perform the corresponding operations. The demonstrations for seamless navigation and zooming in and out for the electronic map to location a selected location were achieved (Movie S2, Supporting Information).

In addition to the navigation of the electronic map, we also developed a game demonstration of Tetris controlled by the IR touch sensor (Figure 5d, Movie S3, Supporting Information). Similar to the working process of the above navigation operation, the IR touch sensor was divided into four channels that could trigger different action instructions of rotation, moving down, moving left, and moving right, respectively. In detail, when a finger slid on the IR touch sensor, the signal was monitored in real time and mapped to the voltage heatmap by calculation (Figure 5d). The results of the voltage heatmap were distinctly differentiated in the tests of sliding four different paths (Figure S19, Supporting Information). Once the preset path was recognized, the system executed the corresponding operations, as shown in Figure 5e. Compared to single-point commands from a mouse or keyboard, sliding gestures aligned more with users’ intuitive hand movements. It simulated the actual sensation of sliding. This not only made it easier for users to comprehend and master game rules but also enhanced the playability of the game. Furthermore, sliding operations introduced additional maneuvers and offered a broader spectrum of interactions and expanded the possibilities for users’ engagement. Collectively, these demonstrations with the IR touch sensors allowed for sensitive and easy detection of human's intent in a variety of scenarios. This capability went beyond simple touch detection, enabling more natural interactions in dynamic environments.

2.5 Machine-Learning-Assisted Tactile Intent Recognition System

Tactile intent recognition systems can establish correlations between tactile information and human intent irrespective of environment factors. Visual and auditory intent recognition systems may be impeded in noisy or visually obscured environments (Figure 6a-i,ii). As a robust alternative, the tactile modality stands out for its effectiveness (Figure 6a-iii). Handwriting recognition is the process of converting the trajectory information, which is generated by writing on handwriting-enabled devices, into textual content. Compared to other input methods, handwriting enabled users to enter text most naturally and comfortably. Therefore, the tactile intent recognition system used for handwriting recognition could enhance the overall user experience and accurately convey the user's ideas. For this reason, a machine-learning-assisted tactile intent recognition system based on the IR touch sensor was designed.

When a finger slid on the IR touch sensor to write 26 letters, corresponding output signals were collected (Figure S20, Supporting Information). Different letters exhibited distinct signal characteristics. The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) provided a clear depiction of the signal frequency with time (Figure 6b). Additionally, it visually conveyed the corresponding amplitude magnitudes through a color representation. Here, five letters “A”, “B”, “X”, “M”, and “U” were studied as examples. STFT was applied to process the signal of the letters (Figure S21, Supporting Information). Figure 6c demonstrated seven mathematical features extracted and analyzed from the signals, including average value, skewness, max, min, kurtosis, interquartile range, and standard deviation (Note S2, Supporting Information). It was preliminary evidence that the signals of each letter possessed their own unique characteristics and could be distinguished using an appropriate machine learning algorithm.

Although differentiating signals based on distinct features was possible, practical applications necessitated the consideration of uncontrollable factors, such as sliding velocity and range. Thus, to ensure the accuracy of intent recognition, it was crucial to apply machine learning algorithms for signal identification.[54] Machine learning is proven to be effective in automating the learning process of signal features from touch sensors. Convolutional neural network (CNN), which is one class of machine learning algorithms, excel in effectively addressing intricate classification challenges with good robustness.[55] The 1D CNN (1D CNN) can effectively capture local relationships within the signal,[41, 55] making it well-suited for recognizing the time-domain signals of handwriting from the IR touch sensor.55 Here, a real-time handwriting recognition system based on the 1D CNN model was developed to achieve accurate intent recognition. Figure 6d presented a flowchart manifesting the details of handwriting recognition using the IR touch sensor with the assistance of a machine learning algorithm. Initially, the collected data were processed and subsequently divided into two groups for training and testing. A machine learning algorithm was employed to identify the characteristics of these data. When the finger wrote letters on the IR touch sensor, the algorithm could recognize the letters correctly by processing the output signal.

To enhance the recognition accuracy of the 1D CNN model, kernel size, the number of filters, and convolutional layers were adjusted to optimize the model structure. In Figure 6e, the 1D CNN model demonstrated optimal accuracy performance with 5 kernels, 32 filters, and 4 convolutional layers. Subsequently, the GridSearchCV method was used to split the training set with fivefold cross-validation to gain the optimal hyperparameters (batch size = 150 and epoch = 64) (Figure S22a, Supporting Information). Figure S22b (Supporting Information) showed the structure diagram of the optimized 1D CNN model, which was used for handwriting recognition. Table S3 (Supporting Information) showed the model's summary. After the training process in the 1D CNN model with 40 training epochs, the maximum accuracy could be achieved (Figure 6f). The result showed that the accuracy of the training set was closer to the validation set, indicating that the issue of over-fitting had been averted. Moreover, the loss values for both training and validation sets gradually converged during the 150 training epochs, demonstrating the robustness of this model. The average recognition accuracy extracted from the confusion matrix was 98.4% (Figure 6g). The letters “A”, “X”, “M”, and “U” were recognized with complete accuracy, while there was a 14% chance of confusing the letter “B” for “A”. Additionally, real-time handwriting recognition was also verified to illustrate the reliability of the 1D CNN model (Figure S22c, Supporting Information). Furthermore, a machine-learning-assisted intelligent handwriting recognition system with a real-time display was developed. It connected the IR touch sensor, Arduino, and self-programmed software. When an experimenter wrote a letter on the IR touch sensor, Arduino collected voltage signals and transmitted them to the 1D CNN model, and simultaneously displayed the output signal on the software. This model, which was based on a pre-trained experience, classified the signal and outputted the corresponding letter on the software. As showcased in Figure 6h and Movie S4 (Supporting Information), the experimenter wrote down ‘X – M – U’ on the IR touch sensor. The corresponding letter and signal of ‘X – M – U’ appeared in real time in the software. Combining machine learning algorithm, the intelligent handwriting recognition system could effectively analyze and interpret the intricate patterns and features present in handwritten input. It would result in improved accuracy in deciphering user intent. Algorithms could capture differences in personal writing styles and the machine-learning-assisted intelligent handwriting recognition system could further extend the scope of interaction.

Parkinson's disease (PD) is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder that can lead to progressive disability and significantly affect the quality of life of those affected.[56] However, there are no valid biomarkers available for the diagnosis or monitoring of PD at present.[57, 58] Neurofunctional assessment plays a crucial role in the diagnosis and intervention of neurological disorders. In clinical practice, assessments are often based on a variety of scales, tests, and questionnaires,[58] but these methods rely on expensive specialized equipment and healthcare professionals. Moreover, these approaches lack the capability for continuous storage and quantitative analysis of key factors throughout the diagnostic process. It will be subject to subjective influence by healthcare professionals. The machine-learning-assisted intelligent handwriting recognition system could capture unconscious behavior as a means of assisting treatment. It provided clinicians with a quantitative and standardized neurofunctional analysis that allowed for a more objective and comprehensive assessment of the PD patient's condition (Figure 6i). Using in-sensor computing technologies and sophisticated algorithms, the intelligent handwriting recognition system could detect subtle patterns and movements of user interactions, providing valuable insights into potential health indicators. Additionally, it could function as a tool for the daily training of PD patients (Figure S23, Supporting Information). They made practice according to predefined test patterns, such as the trail-making test, the graph copying test, and so on. After completing the training sessions, the relevant information would be sent to the doctor for training evaluation. In short, the intelligent handwriting recognition system could achieve multiple functions, including health screening, clinical diagnosis, and rehabilitation monitoring for neural health, which would make a good promise for smart healthcare.

3 Conclusion

In summary, we designed an event-driven and in-sensor computing monolithic IR touch sensor web with scalable resolutions, which was inspired by the spiral structure of a spider web, for human intent recognition. Biomimetic helical web, by connecting separated pixel points, innovatively combined low data dimension and ultrahigh precision spatiotemporal resolution into the same device at the device level. The design of the biomimetic helical web authentically overcame the critical challenges posed by numerous discrete sensing units and allowed the device to scale the resolution extension based on application requirements while maintaining a constant number of electrodes. The IR touch sensor utilized “external stimulation” as the event that drove the start of data acquisition and transmission. Benefiting from the event-driven operating mechanism, the IR touch sensor could avoid generating a large amount of meaningless data during standby. The preliminary data was processed within the IR touch sensor, which integrated spatial information into a temporal signal in the form of amplitude features and directly output a 1D fusion signal. This in-sensor computing capability minimized the transfer of redundant data between the sensing units and computing terminal and reduced the complexity of data processing and conversion, streamlining the processing of sensing information and facilitating real-time analysis and decision-making. The output signal of the IR touch sensor achieved the successful extraction of action trajectories, which proved the superiority of the IR touch sensor compared to the commercial resistive touch screen. This feature verified that the IR touch sensor achieved a perfect balance between concise data and accurate intent recognition, providing an innovative and effective solution for motion detection and bringing an important breakthrough in the field of intent recognition. Tactile intent recognitions using the IR touch sensor were enough to work in all-weather surroundings regardless of shading, dynamics, darkness, and noise, which were demonstrated by versatile applications. Due to the bending insensitivity and sliding decoupling advantage of the IR touch sensor, sliding or pressing operations were accurately decoded based on the output signals, offering accurate instructions for scenarios, such as controlling PowerPoint presentations, navigation tasks, and gaming interactions. Through machine learning algorithms, hidden action features were extracted, proving the ultrahigh recognition accuracy of 98.4% to capture human motion, even unconscious behavior. Its use as a competitive means of adjunct judgment demonstrated the practicability of the IR touch sensor for the diagnosis of neurological disorders. The IR touch sensor with scalable resolution, event-driven operating mechanism, and in-sensor computing capability will greatly expand applications in various intent-recognition scenarios from virtual reality and augmented reality to various interactions in artificial intelligence of things.

4 Experimental Section

Fabrication of the IR Touch Sensor

A polyethylene terephthalate (PET) (Foshan Wencheng Materials Co., Ltd., thickness of 20 µm) film was chosen as the substrate of the conductive pattern. At first, the PET film was washed with absolute ethanol and deionized water for 10 min to remove residue and dust. The conductive ink was prepared by mixing conductive carbon paste (DELIO, JW-001) well with diluent (DELIO, 783-A) in a weight ratio of 10:1. Then, a part of the PET was covered with a spiral pattern by conductive ink through screen-printing to prepare the upper conductive pattern. The printed conductive pattern was subsequently cured for 10 min at 60 °C and then cool to room temperature. There was the same way to obtain the bottom conductive pattern. It should be noted that the pattern printed on the upper and bottom substrate was mirror symmetric. Two conductive lines were respectively drawn out from the conductive patterns by silver paint (SPI-PAINT, Structure Probe, Inc.). Coated PET (Jiaxing Youjun paper products shop) was attached to both sides of the double-sided tape for the preparation of a patterned spacer. A laser cutting machine was utilized at a current power of 25 W and a cutting speed of 15 mm s−1 to create a hollow pattern on the based spacer, which should match the screen-printing pattern on the PET. Finally, the upper and bottom conductive patterns were placed face-to-face together by the patterned spacer and the hollow pattern was aligned with the printed pattern to prevent the ink from changing due to unintentional touching.

Characterization and Measurement

The morphology was characterized using the field emission scanning electron microscope (SUPRA55 SAPPHIRE). The surface height topography of the conductive pattern was measured using a shape measurement laser microscope from Keyence (VK-X1000). The customized actuator executed cyclic dynamic touching and sliding tests on the IR touch sensor (Beijing Times Brilliant Electric Technology Co. Ltd). The control panel of the programmable actuator was used to set the loading time, interval, and number of the cyclic dynamic external stimulation. The response value, including resistance, voltage, and current of the IR touch sensor, was recorded by the testing by digital multimeters (Proskit MT-1236 and Keysight 34465A). The thickness of the spacer was measured by the vernier caliper (K20K271592, GuangLu Digital measurement and control Technology Co. Ltd.). To assess the response time and recovery time of the IR touch sensor, the oscilloscope (GW instek MFG-2220HM) was used.

Statistical Analysis

Origin (2022 version) was used to analyze the measured signals. MATLAB (2022b version) was used for short-time Fourier transform of handwritten signals. The sample size (n) for each statistical analysis was five. In cases where the data was displayed as a box plot, the horizontal line represented the median value, the lower and upper quartiles represented the 25th and 75th percentile, and the whiskers showed the maximum and minimum values.
